query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In an oxidizing high-temperature environment, increasing the oxygen partial pressure causes the formation of a continuous oxide surface layer on the as‐built FCC-structured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA. This surface oxidation suppresses the beneficial FCC-to-HCP phase transformation (that normally accommodates plastic deformation) and instead triggers the preferential nucleation of brittle BCC phases within the matrix, thereby reducing ductility and ultimately leading to catastrophic failure under mechanical loading.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy in the as‐built state, characterized by a homogeneous FCC matrix with minimal pre-existing brittle phases.
generation.intervention: Systematic variation of the gas environment by modulating the oxygen partial pressure during high-temperature exposure while keeping temperature, exposure time, and other conditions constant.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperature (e.g., around 800 °C) exposures for extended durations in controlled atmospheres, varying between moderately oxidizing (e.g., ambient oxygen partial pressure or higher) and reducing gas environments.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and continuity of an oxide surface layer that alters dislocation nucleation and phase transformation pathways within the alloy.
generation.mechanism: Under higher oxygen partial pressures, surface oxidation suppresses the nucleation of Shockley partial dislocations and thus inhibits the FCC-to-HCP transformation that typically enhances ductility. Instead, the altered surface chemistry promotes the nucleation of a brittle BCC phase in the FCC matrix, leading to an increase in elastic modulus but a decrease in overall ductility. This brittle phase accumulation is posited to be the precursor to catastrophic failure when mechanical stress is applied.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as‐built state, samples exposed in an oxidizing environment will exhibit increased BCC phase fractions, a higher elastic modulus, and reduced ductility. In contrast, samples exposed under reducing conditions should retain more of the original FCC microstructure along with a more pronounced FCC-to-HCP transformation, preserving ductility and delaying catastrophic failure.
generation.baseline: The as‐built HEA before any high-temperature gas exposure, characterized by a homogeneous FCC matrix with minimal oxide formation and balanced plastic deformation via dislocation activity.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable for exposures at temperatures around 800 °C in gas environments where the oxygen partial pressure is at or above ambient levels, and over durations sufficient to allow surface oxidation (e.g., several hours). It may not apply at significantly lower temperatures or at oxygen levels that do not support continuous oxide layer formation.
generation.uncertainty: The precise oxygen partial pressure threshold that triggers the switch from FCC-to-HCP to FCC-to-BCC transformation and the kinetics of the oxide layer formation are not fully quantified and may vary with processing history and microstructural heterogeneities.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple specimens of the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA and subject them to high-temperature (800 °C) exposure under controlled gas atmospheres. One set is exposed under an oxidizing environment with a high oxygen partial pressure (at or above ambient), while a control set is exposed under a reducing atmosphere. All other parameters (temperature, duration, etc.) should be held constant.
measurements: Microstructural characterization (e.g., via XRD and TEM) to quantify the phase fractions (FCC, HCP, and BCC phases).
Surface chemical analysis (e.g., XPS or EDS) to confirm the presence and continuity of oxide layers.
Mechanical testing (tensile tests) to measure elastic modulus and ductility.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxidizing condition does not result in a statistically significant increase in the BCC phase fraction along with a corresponding increase in elastic modulus and reduction in ductility (or if similar phase transformations and mechanical properties occur in both oxidizing and reducing environments), the hypothesis that surface oxidation under high oxygen partial pressure governs the pathway to catastrophic failure by favoring BCC formation will be rejected.

The fast growth of MnO should be kinetically favourable because of its highly unstable nature. The high-temperature oxidation of Mn to MnO, i.e., 700 °C instead of 550 °C (during HTXRD in air), can be explained by lower oxygen partial pressure. With an increase in oxidation temperature and exposure time, MnO phase peaks’ intensity progressively increased, which indicates Mn’s continuous oxidation. Quantitative analysis of the data revealed a gradual increase in the second phase due to the fast formation of MnO. As Mn has a higher affinity for oxygen, with an increase in temperature, Mn preferentially diffuses from inside to the surface and thus reacts with oxygen. AbstractHigh entropy alloys (HEAs) have demonstrated excellent potential in various applications owing to the unique properties. One of the most critical issues of HEAs is the stress corrosion cracking (SCC) which limits its reliability in practical applications. However, the SCC mechanisms have not been fully understood yet because of the difficulty of experimental measuring of atomic-scale deformation mechanisms and surface reactions. In this work, we conduct atomistic uniaxial tensile simulations using an FCC-type Fe40Ni40Cr20 alloy as a typical simplification of normal HEAs, in order to reveal how a corrosive environment such as high-temperature/pressure water affects the tensile behaviors and deformation mechanisms. In a vacuum, we observe the generation of layered HCP phases in an FCC matrix during tensile simulation induced by the formation of Shockley partial dislocations from surface and grain boundaries. While, in the corrosive environment of high-temperature/pressure water, the alloy surface is oxidized by chemical reactions with water and this oxide surface layer can suppress the formation of Shockley partial dislocation as well as the resulting FCC-to-HCP phase transit

In this work, uniaxial tensile simulations of FCC-type Fe40Ni40Cr20 alloy (as a simplified model of HEAs) are conducted in vacuum and high-temperature/pressure water environment to clarify the effect of corrosive environment on the deformation mechanisms. In vacuum, layered HCP phases are formed from FCC matrix during tensile simulation due to the generation of Shockley partial dislocations from surface and grain boundary. While, in the corrosive water environment, alloy surface is oxidized by the reactions with water and this oxidized surface layer can suppress the generation of Shockley partial dislocation as well as the resulted FCC-to-HCP phase transition; instead, generation of BCC phase is preferred to release the tensile stress and stored elastic energy, leading to an enhanced elastic modulus and reduced ductility. Thus, we revealed that the deformation mechanism of Fe40Ni40Cr20 alloy is changed by the presence of high-temperature/pressure water environment—from FCC-to-HCP phase transition in vacuum to FCC-to-BCC phase transition in water. This study as a theoretical fundamental may contribute to the further improvement of HEAs with high resistance to SCC in experiments.

frame.system: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an FCC matrix in its as-built microstructural state
frame.goal: Formulate and test a mechanistic hypothesis that explains how degradation occurs during prolonged exposure to oxidizing and reducing gases at elevated temperatures, and link this degradation mechanism to the onset of catastrophic failure
frame.limitation: The controlling degradation mechanism under high-temperature gas exposure is not well defined, and the specific pathway leading to sudden catastrophic failure remains unclear
constraints: A controlled change (e.g., an intentional modification of gas composition or oxidation state) must be identified that can reveal the dominant degradation behavior
The hypothesis should predict specific microstructural, compositional, or mechanical changes relative to the baseline as-built state
Exposure boundaries (temperature range, gas composition limits, time scales) need to be clearly defined
A clear falsification criterion must be set to reject the hypothesis if the predicted behavior does not occur
frame.regime: Elevated temperature conditions in well-controlled oxidizing and reducing environments (with defined temperature, time, and gas composition parameters)
prior_attempts: Previous studies on similar HEA systems have evaluated thermal stability and oxidation resistance, but lacked a systematic coupling of gas environment variations to mechanistic changes, leading to ambiguity in how oxidation/reduction kinetics contribute to degradation
Early experiments often focused separately on assembly microstructural evolution or macroscopic failure without linking the two scales

decision.trend: Early studies on additively manufactured high-entropy alloys primarily focused on characterizing the as‐built microstructures and the appearance of fine precipitates (e.g., nitrides or intermetallic phases) during thermal exposure. In parallel, separate investigations addressing degradation under reactive environments used atomistic simulations to reveal that surface reactions—with, for example, oxidizing agents—can alter dislocation nucleation and phase transformation pathways (e.g., suppression of beneficial FCC-to-HCP transitions and promotion of more brittle phase formation). While individual studies either examined gas-induced microstructural evolution or the mechanical consequences of such transformations, the integrated mechanistic picture linking controlled gas composition changes to catastrophic failure remains incomplete.
decision.unsolved: The unresolved issue is identifying which specific chemical interactions (oxidation vs. reduction) dominate the degradation process at elevated temperatures and how these interactions trigger a transformation in the alloy’s dislocation and phase behavior that culminates in catastrophic failure. In other words, the community still lacks a testable, controlled hypothesis that directly connects variations in gas composition to measurable microstructural, compositional, and mechanical changes relative to the as‐built state, including clear exposure boundaries and a falsification criterion.
decision.lever: Systematically varying the gas environment by modulating oxygen (or oxidizer/reducer) partial pressure during high-temperature exposure while holding temperature, time, and other parameters constant.
decision.why: This approach follows the trend of first establishing the role of gas environment in modifying microstructural evolution, as seen in atomistic simulation studies, while previous work on additively manufactured HEAs observed reactive phase formation under nitrogen/oxidizing atmospheres. By intentionally altering the gas composition, one can directly test whether an increased oxygen partial pressure suppresses favorable dislocation slip (or phase transitions) and promotes the nucleation of brittle phases, thereby linking the controlled variable (gas composition) to catastrophic failure. A clear baseline and falsification criterion (i.e., if no change in phase behavior or mechanical degradation is observed relative to the as‐built state under altered gas conditions) would then validate or refute the hypothesis.
